Lesson 82: When to Use Single vs. Multi-agent Systems

Deciding between a single agent or multi-agent setup comes down to what best fits your current use case. In certain cases, the simplicity of a single agent structure is more effective, especially when managing well-defined processes that don't demand input from multiple specialists.

Core Concept

Deciding between a single agent or multi-agent setup comes down to what best fits your current use case. In certain cases, the simplicity of a single agent structure is more effective, especially when managing well-defined processes that don't demand input from multiple specialists. Think of it like this.

Key Points

  • In a company, a social media manager can independently create and publish an Instagram post.
  • But launching an omnichannel marketing campaign is an entirely different matter, typically involving collaboration among a copywriter, graphic designer, ads specialist and marketing manager.
  • When a social media manager independently creates and publishes an Instagram post, the task is simple enough for one skilled individual to handle.
  • In contrast, launching an omnichannel marketing campaign introduces far more complexity, requiring a team of specialists whose combined expertise can deliver a high quality result.
  • Another advantage of single agents is that they avoid some of the pitfalls that arise in multi-agent setups when multiple agents collaborate.
  • There's a risk that they might distract one another.
  • Duplicate efforts on the same activity or provide poor feedback to each other's work.
  • The main challenge AI engineers must address when working with a single agent is preventing it from getting stuck in an endless execution loop.
💡 From the Lecture
Deciding between a single agent or multi-agent setup comes down to what best fits your current use case.
💡 From the Lecture
For instance, imagine a translator agent faced with a 300 page document.
Key Takeaways
  • Ten people can accomplish the task faster than one.
  • Research also shows that multi-agent systems tend to perform better in zero shot scenarios, when no examples are provided in the system prompt.
  • Choosing between single and multi-agent designs goes beyond reasoning capabilities.
  • It's about the broader context, the tasks, nature, time constraints, and available resources.

Lesson 83: Vertical vs Horizontal Architectures

When considering multi-agent systems. A key architecture distinction lies between vertical and horizontal designs. In a vertical architecture, a single leader directs the group, with all other agents reporting directly to that leader.

Core Concept

When considering multi-agent systems. A key architecture distinction lies between vertical and horizontal designs. In a vertical architecture, a single leader directs the group, with all other agents reporting directly to that leader.

Key Points

  • In some cases, agents will talk exclusively with their manager.
  • In other instances, they will communicate with each other in a shared conversation, but the lead will assign tasks and approve the outputs of individual agents.
  • Vertical architecture typically has lower latency for decision making because there's a clear leader assigning tasks and approving outputs.
  • Communication flows in a defined path so you avoid the overhead of full group discussions.
  • The key characteristics of the vertical architecture choice include a clear division of labor, and a single figure responsible for assigning work to individual agents.
  • A horizontal architecture, by contrast, features a flat structure where all agents are equal and communicate through a shared thread.
  • Each agent can assess and read every message, ensuring complete and mutual awareness.
  • Delegation occurs through a volunteering mechanism where agents volunteer to complete tasks.
💡 From the Lecture
The key characteristics of the vertical architecture choice include a clear division of labor, and a single figure responsible for assigning work to individual agents.
💡 From the Lecture
The key is to align the architecture with the tasks requirements, achieving the best balance between efficiency and output quality.
Key Takeaways
  • In summary, the choice between a vertical or horizontal multi-agent architecture ultimately depends on your specific objectives.
  • A vertical setup provides structure and ensures clear guidance throughout the entire process.
  • A horizontal setup promotes openness, enabling agents to collaborate equally and exchange ideas freely.
  • The key is to align the architecture with the tasks requirements, achieving the best balance between efficiency and output quality.

Lesson 84: Challenges with Group Conversations

A single agent stays focused without being distracted by external input. On the contrary, it remains focused, completing the task using its own abilities and the available information. That focus is a considerable advantage over multi-agent architectures, which often face challenges with group conversation and information sharing in a horizontal architecture.

Core Concept

A single agent stays focused without being distracted by external input. On the contrary, it remains focused, completing the task using its own abilities and the available information. That focus is a considerable advantage over multi-agent architectures, which often face challenges with group conversation and information sharing in a horizontal architecture.

Key Points

  • Agents often end up wasting time on unnecessary chatter and pleasantries when multiple agents read the same thread.
  • It can result in inefficient resource use and higher latency.
  • Agents might waste time on casual exchanges like how are you?
  • Instead of focusing on advancing the task.
  • To address this issue, AI engineers use robust, prompt engineering that forbids distractions and unnecessary conversations that don't contribute to the task at hand.
  • In a vertical architecture, the risk of distractions is much lower since agents communicate directly with the lead agent.
  • But since agents don't communicate directly with one another, there may be instances where subordinate agents lack the information needed to perform their tasks effectively.
  • This can be problematic and could lead to confusion and even hallucination in some instances.
Key Takeaways
  • But since agents don't communicate directly with one another, there may be instances where subordinate agents lack the information needed to perform their tasks effectively.
  • This can be problematic and could lead to confusion and even hallucination in some instances.
  • The solution is to define access permissions in the system prompt, enabling subordinate agents to receive the necessary information.
  • These are two considerations to keep in mind when working with multi-agent architectures, whether in a horizontal or vertical setup.

Lesson 86: Hierarchical Teams

We just explored the supervisor architecture, a structure where a single agent acts as the supervisor, managing several subordinate agents, assigning tasks, offering feedback, and reviewing their output.

Core Concept

We just explored the supervisor architecture, a structure where a single agent acts as the supervisor, managing several subordinate agents, assigning tasks, offering feedback, and reviewing their output. A real life analogy would be a small firm where a manager supervises a team of employees. In this type of business, there's limited specialization so the manager can effectively oversee the work of 4 or 5 employees, sometimes even as many as 7 or 8.

Key Points

  • But as the business continues to grow, it eventually reaches a point where a new organizational structure is needed to manage operations effectively.
  • A single manager cannot effectively supervise 20 or 30 people.
  • The workload becomes unmanageable, communication deteriorates, and quality control begins to decline.
  • At that stage, the business usually evolves into a more layered structure where the original manager delegates oversight to other managers.
  • This creates a hierarchical chain of command.
  • Likewise, when handling tasks that require coordinating many agents, a single agent may not be capable of effectively managing them all.
  • Moreover, it could be beneficial if manager agents are also specialized in the task the team has been assigned.
  • Consider a hierarchical team of agents that can create a marketing campaign from scratch.

Key Takeaways
  • The managers would then report to a supervising manager who oversees the entire operation, maintaining the big picture perspective, coordinating the efforts of all specialized teams, and ensuring that everything aligns with the campaign's overall goals.
  • In other words, while each specialized manager focuses on excellence within their own domain, the supervisor manager ensures coordination across domains, resolves conflicts between teams, and manages timelines and priorities at the project level.
  • The hierarchical team architecture is suitable for complex and comprehensive use cases.
  • This structure improves scalability, communication and quality control, but it also demands careful planning to prevent bottlenecks at the top and ensure that accurate information flows smoothly through each layer.

Lesson 87: Dynamic Teams

Next, we'll consider dynamic teams a flexible and adaptive pattern where teams are assembled, disassembled, and reconfigured as needed. Core Concept

Next, we'll consider dynamic teams a flexible and adaptive pattern where teams are assembled, disassembled, and reconfigured as needed. The dynamic reassignment feature of this architecture is useful in situations where agents need to be added or removed from the system, depending on current needs and workload. We should remember that even though the composition of dynamic teams changes, they continue to have an authority layer that assigns tasks.

Key Points

  • For this reason, dynamic teams are a vertical type of architecture.
  • Some might argue that dynamic teams don't follow a strictly vertical hierarchy, especially when teams are disbanded and all agents return to a shared pool without fixed reporting lines.
  • At that point, the structure becomes more horizontal, wouldn't you say?
  • For a short while, agents become peers and interact as equals.
  • But soon after, when a new team configuration is formed, the vertical layer of authority naturally reemerges.
  • Therefore, since dynamic teams operate within a vertical structure most of the time, particularly during their most productive phases, we can also classify this type of architecture as vertical.

Lesson 89: Agents and Asyncronous Task Execution

What's the most effective way to speed up a task that involves a lot of hands on work? Get more people working on it in parallel. In many real world tasks, if one person handles everything sequentially, the overall pace is limited by that individual's speed.

Core Concept

What's the most effective way to speed up a task that involves a lot of hands on work? Get more people working on it in parallel. In this lesson, we'll use this idea to explore asynchronous task execution and highlight the key difference between single and multi-agent systems.

Key Points

  • In many real world tasks, if one person handles everything sequentially, the overall pace is limited by that individual's speed.
  • But if you can split up the work into several parts and involve multiple people working on them simultaneously, you can often finish much faster.
  • Synchronous execution means an agent waits for one task to finish before starting the next.
  • Asynchronous execution allows tasks to run in parallel without blocking one another if they don't rely on each other's results.
  • Imagine a baker preparing ten cakes alone.
  • They start by measuring ingredients, mixing the batter, baking and decorating.
  • Completing each step for cake number one before moving on to cake number two.
  • While the baker mixes, the oven sits unused while the cakes bake the counter and tools sit idle.
💡 From the Lecture
In this lesson, we'll use this idea to explore asynchronous task execution and highlight the key difference between single and multi-agent systems.
💡 From the Lecture
In many real world tasks, if one person handles everything sequentially, the overall pace is limited by that individual's speed.
Key Takeaways
  • In multi-agent setups, different agents often handle separate subtasks independently, with a coordinator agent combining their outputs.
  • Naturally, the advantage of asynchronous execution with multiple agents is its ability to reduce latency.
  • Moreover, this approach enables scalability because this type of structure prepares the AI agent system for larger workloads.
  • We should remember, however, that not all tasks can benefit from async execution if the intermediate steps needed to solve the task at hand require results that depend on the previous step, we cannot rely on asynchronous execution.

Lesson 90: Performance Metrics - Latency and Cost

When agents are deployed in a live environment. Two key questions to ask are one how fast is the solution we've launched? And two how much does it cost to operate? Ideally, before going live, we've confirmed that the agent can solve the intended problem.

Core Concept

When agents are deployed in a live environment. Two key questions to ask are one how fast is the solution we've launched? And two how much does it cost to operate?

Key Points

  • Ideally, before going live, we've confirmed that the agent can solve the intended problem.
  • Now it's time to assess whether it can do so efficiently.
  • Staying within the performance and budget constraints of a real world environment, latency can be divided into two main components model interference latency and orchestration.
  • Model interference depends on the type of model you select for your agent system.
  • Generally, larger models exhibit higher latency, and the prompt length you send to the model also plays a significant role.
  • For example, a GPT five call with a long chain of thought may take several seconds, while a GPT four turbo call on a short prompt may return in under a second beyond the model's response time.
  • These delays can arise from processes like chaining prompts, waiting for parallel tasks to complete, performing memory lookups from a vector database, calling external APIs or tools, or coordinating multiple agents.
  • In practice, orchestration overhead can be just as significant as model response time, sometimes even larger, especially in multi-agent systems.
💡 From the Lecture
Staying within the performance and budget constraints of a real world environment, latency can be divided into two main components model interference latency and orchestration.
💡 From the Lecture

Key Takeaways
  • These considerations determine the runtime efficiency of the agent system we've designed today.
  • It takes significant experience and AI engineering effort to design a truly optimized system.
  • AI engineers continually evaluate latency cost trade offs across different scenarios to determine the most effective course of action.
  • The key takeaway is that building effective agents isn't just about solving the problem, it's about doing it efficiently.

Lesson 91: Error Handling and Recovery

The latency and cost optimization performance metrics we examined in the previous lesson are intended for situations where the agent system works as intended. This means the agent can accomplish its intended goals while striving to achieve optimal performance.

Core Concept

The latency and cost optimization performance metrics we examined in the previous lesson are intended for situations where the agent system works as intended. This means the agent can accomplish its intended goals while striving to achieve optimal performance. But sometimes things don't go as planned.

Key Points

  • That's when error handling and recovery matter most.
  • To accomplish their goals, agents depend on several interconnected components.
  • They draw reasoning from an Lem, connect to external tools through APIs, and in some cases receive input from other agents.
  • So naturally, the more sophisticated a structure, the higher the chances of failures.
  • It may not happen all the time, but it does occur at least occasionally.
  • LMS may go offline for maintenance or produce unexpected outputs, while external tools can experience temporary outages or return incomplete data.
  • External agents can miscommunicate and many other issues can arise along the way.
  • This is why robust error handling and recovery mechanisms are essential parts of any production ready agent architecture.
💡 From the Lecture
This means the agent can accomplish its intended goals while striving to achieve optimal performance.

For instance, you could implement retry logic for failed LM calls or even route requests to an alternative LM.
Key Takeaways
  • Similar procedures can be created for other parts of the system, such as APIs and agent to agent communication.
  • Ultimately, the goal isn't to eliminate every error that's unrealistic, but to ensure the system can fail gracefully and continue progressing towards its objectives without a complete breakdown.
  • We want to ensure that the end user's experience remains smooth and uninterrupted, even when specific components are unavailable or performing below optimal levels.
  • Designing reliable error handling and recovery mechanisms is one of the most complex and demanding challenges in AI engineering, requiring substantial effort in every project you undertake.

Lesson 93: Short-term Context Buffer

The most basic type of memory we can give an AI agent is known as a short term context buffer. This enables the AI agent to retain and reference a limited number of recent interactions. Imagine you've built a chatbot that's powered by one of OpenAI's GPT models.

Core Concept

The most basic type of memory we can give an AI agent is known as a short term context buffer. This enables the AI agent to retain and reference a limited number of recent interactions. Imagine you've built a chatbot that's powered by one of OpenAI's GPT models.

Key Points

  • Interestingly, the OpenAI API doesn't include built in memory by default.
  • Each API call is stateless and forgets prior interactions unless you explicitly provide the previous context in your request.
  • If you were to design a short term memory mechanism, you'd essentially decide to retain the last, let's say, ten messages and include them again with each new request.
  • In this setup, the agent remembers only the ten most recent messages.
  • Once the conversation goes beyond that limit, it forgets earlier exchanges.
  • That's one of the key limitations of short term context memory.
  • Once the buffer overflows, the forgotten content is lost for good.
  • The agent can access only what fits within its defined context window.
💡 From the Lecture
Imagine you've built a chatbot that's powered by one of OpenAI's GPT models.

Key Takeaways
  • Because the agent only retains limited information, it can respond quickly and handle each conversation with a relatively clear mind.
  • The limitation is obvious, right when you need more context and longer term memory.
  • This approach is not sufficient.
  • That's why more advanced methods like vector stores and entity level memory are needed for long term context.

Lesson 94: Vector store RAG

The key drawback of short term memory is that it doesn't allow our agent to store a significant number of past interactions. Ideally, the agent should be capable of continuing a conversation exactly where it left off, drawing on a rich store of knowledge to make the interaction feel more natural and contextually relevant.

Core Concept

The key drawback of short term memory is that it doesn't allow our agent to store a significant number of past interactions. Ideally, the agent should be capable of continuing a conversation exactly where it left off, drawing on a rich store of knowledge to make the interaction feel more natural and contextually relevant. Someone with a good memory can recall past experiences and respond to questions about things they learned long ago.

Key Points

  • Similarly, for an agent to appear truly intelligent, it must be able to recall past interactions and use that knowledge to deliver more accurate and insightful responses.
  • Rather than starting from scratch each time, it should build on what has already been discussed.
  • Just as humans rely on memory to keep conversations coherent and meaningful, we need a method that makes this possible.
  • And that's where Vector Store Rag comes in.
  • You may already know this, but Rag stands for retrieval Augmented Generation.
  • Put simply, it's a technique that retrieves relevant information from existing knowledge sources and feeds it to an LLM, helping the model to generate more accurate and insightful responses.
  • Think of a company developing a chatbot for internal use.
  • Its purpose is to help employees get answers to questions about company policies, privacy guidelines, and HR procedures.

This is done by converting the information into vectors, essentially translating text into numerical representations that the model can understand and work with.
Key Takeaways
  • The system doesn't necessarily supply the language model with the most relevant information needed to generate the best possible response.
  • Moreover, searching through thousands of pages can add significant latency to your project in some instances.
  • Rag represents a significant step toward building agents that can genuinely remember and apply knowledge in a way that feels intelligent.
  • In the next lesson, we'll explore entity level memory, which expands on this foundation to enable more personalized and context aware interactions.

Lesson 95: Entity-level Memory

The third type of memory we'll cover is entity level memory. This type of memory focuses on retaining information about specific entities such as people, companies, or products. For example, imagine a chatbot installed as an app on your phone.

Core Concept

The third type of memory we'll cover is entity level memory. This type of memory focuses on retaining information about specific entities such as people, companies, or products. For example, imagine a chatbot installed as an app on your phone.

Key Points

  • Entity level memory is designed to learn about you, your preferences, habits, and past interactions, allowing it to personalize responses and adapt over time.
  • Each time you add information about yourself in your conversations with the chatbot, the agent will add this information to its knowledge repository.
  • So the next time you interact with it, the agent will consider the information it previously stored before generating a response.
  • This allows the agent to provide much more thoughtful responses.
  • Let's say you're chatting with a bot that uses entity level memory, and you've mentioned that you live in Italy.
  • The next time you ask the agent about the weather, it will already know to show the temperature in Celsius.
  • This type of memory is focused on providing a personalized experience over time.
  • It can be beneficial in a business context when the industry and product you work on remain stable.

Lesson 97: Self-reflection

Every problem is solved through a sequence of small reasoning steps, each comparable to a single move in the overall thinking process. On Monday morning, I need to decide whether to commute to the office by car or by bicycle.

Core Concept

Every problem is solved through a sequence of small reasoning steps, each comparable to a single move in the overall thinking process. On Monday morning, I need to decide whether to commute to the office by car or by bicycle. There are several factors I'll take into account one.

Key Points

  • I'll remember that Mondays usually have heavy traffic.
  • Two next, I'll compare the car and the bicycle, concluding that traffic would delay me by about 15 minutes.
  • If I choose to drive three, then comes calculation.
  • I'll estimate the time needed to park the car near the office versus the time required to lock up the bike.
  • In this case, the bike is the faster option once again, so I'll go ahead and eliminate the car as an option.
  • I'll also recall that if I take the bicycle, I won't be able to go to the gym afterward.
  • See how many small intermediate reasoning steps I used for this decision.
  • The self-reflection planning method enables agents to determine the most effective way to solve complex problems independently.
💡 From the Lecture
I'll remember that Mondays usually have heavy traffic.
Key Takeaways
  • But by incorporating comparison, calculation, elimination, and an additional recall step, I arrived at a more well-considered conclusion.
  • That's precisely how self-discovery works in Llms.
  • Instead of using a single reasoning style, it can assemble a chain of small reasoning steps tailored to the specific problem.
  • This makes the model more flexible as the agent figures out the optimal course of action automatically.

Lesson 98: Human-in-the-loop

Do you remember studying math in high school? Sometimes you'd start a problem with the wrong assumption, and every step after that would be affected by the end. The teacher no longer deducted points for a single mistake.

Core Concept

Do you remember studying math in high school? Sometimes you'd start a problem with the wrong assumption, and every step after that would be affected by the end. The teacher no longer deducted points for a single mistake.

Key Points

  • Instead, they often marked the entire solution as wrong.
  • AI agents often face a similar challenge.
  • They tend to commit to a solution prematurely without adequately exploring the best approach.
  • Once an LLM begins reasoning down the wrong path, the error can snowball, producing a final result that diverges significantly from the intended outcome.
  • In such instances, it's beneficial if the AI agent can receive guidance.
  • Such help can come in two forms one through self-reflection as discussed in the previous lesson, or two through feedback from a human.
  • People possess specialized skills and intuition that make them far better at correcting an agent's course and helping the AI reach its goal.
  • Moreover, human directions help the AI produce a result that aligns with human expectations.
💡 From the Lecture
Do you remember studying math in high school?
Key Takeaways
  • Human involvement provides a critical safeguard, ensuring that the agent's reasoning remains aligned with reality.
  • Moreover, we shouldn't forget that it's always best practice to add a human in the loop.
  • Human oversight can help agents recover when they reach a dead end or become trapped in repetitive reasoning.
  • By offering external feedback or correction, a human can redirect the agent's reasoning and help it continue toward a productive solution.

Lesson 100: Guardrails and Policy Enforcement

Why do we need guardrails on roads? They prevent cars from veering off cliffs. This approach reduces the risk for drivers. But it's not the only mechanism that does so. There are also speed limits that regulate how fast drivers can travel, reducing the likelihood of losing control.

Core Concept

Why do we need guardrails on roads? They prevent cars from veering off cliffs. This approach reduces the risk for drivers.

Key Points

  • But it's not the only mechanism that does so.
  • There are also speed limits that regulate how fast drivers can travel, reducing the likelihood of losing control.
  • Similarly, traffic lights guide the flow of vehicles, minimizing collisions at intersections.
  • Road signs provide critical information about hazards ahead, enabling drivers to anticipate and avoid danger.
  • So road safety is created by combining several layered mechanisms.
  • While a single mechanism is unlikely to provide sufficient protection, using multiple specialized mechanisms together improves the system as a whole and helps mitigate risks.
  • Similarly, when creating AI agents, we must ensure that necessary guardrails for protection are in place.
  • The goal is to mitigate risk when the AI agent is deployed in real life applications.
💡 From the Lecture
Once an AI agent is deployed in real world situations, new edges will inevitably emerge, requiring you to update and refine its guardrails continually.
Key Takeaways
  • Always decline requests that violate company policies or ethical standards.
  • Building robust guardrails is an ongoing process, one that's never truly finished.
  • Once an AI agent is deployed in real world situations, new edges will inevitably emerge, requiring you to update and refine its guardrails continually.
  • Of course, careful planning and thorough refinement of guardrails during development will help ensure that the AI agent behaves more safely and reliably from the start.

Lesson 101: Cost-limiter

If there's one thing that makes businesses uneasy, it's cost uncertainty. The thought of deploying a solution that consumes resources 24 over seven, while having little idea what the month end bill will be until it arrives, must be unsettling for management.

Core Concept

If there's one thing that makes businesses uneasy, it's cost uncertainty. The thought of deploying a solution that consumes resources 24 over seven, while having little idea what the month end bill will be until it arrives, must be unsettling for management. This is vastly different from what they've seen so far.

Key Points

  • With traditional software cost limiter execution time can vary, but within acceptable limits.
  • The cost of development personnel remains relatively stable, while deployment and maintenance expenses are minimal compared to the initial investment.
  • As a result, company executives can gauge their costs with a high degree of certainty before getting started.
  • This isn't necessarily true for AI agents, which operate 24 over seven.
  • One of their key advantages and can make thousands of API and LM calls each day.
  • They can get stuck in a loop over query APIs and generate strange and expensive outputs.
  • To address this issue, AI engineers must design systems with safeguards that prevent agents from incurring excessive costs without explicit authorization.
  • This technique, known as cost limiter, acts as a governance mechanism that ensures the agent operates within a predefined budget.
💡 From the Lecture
All of this means higher bills.
💡 From the Lecture
In practice, the cost limiter can be set for the agent in terms of tokens, dollars, or the number of API calls.
Key Takeaways
  • And what happens when an agent reaches its spending limit?
  • It shuts down gracefully and delivers a helpful fallback response, letting the user know it cannot continue.
  • For example, suppose this occurs with a call service agent once the cost limiter is reached during a conversation.
  • In that case, the agent can escalate the interaction to a human operator to take over.

Lesson 102: A/B Shadow Testing

Customers are using it, and you observe their interactions and gain valuable insights on what could be improved. After a while, it becomes evident that the AI agent needs a few tweaks. This type of system, however, is far from an exact science.

Core Concept

Let's say your AI agent is already deployed in production. Customers are using it, and you observe their interactions and gain valuable insights on what could be improved. After a while, it becomes evident that the AI agent needs a few tweaks.

Key Points

  • This type of system, however, is far from an exact science.
  • New versions don't always guarantee better performance, and when clients interact with the product in real life situations, you don't want to risk degrading their experience by rolling out an unproven update.
  • This is where AB shadow testing comes into play.
  • As with a typical AB test, we'll compare two versions, the original A and the new version B, but to ensure the user experience remains unchanged, we won't display the new version to users.
  • Everyone will continue seeing the original version.
  • The new version will exist only in the background, running in a shadow environment.
  • The agent receives user inputs and produces outputs, but those outputs remain hidden from the end users.
  • Instead, they're logged and compared with the original versions.
💡 From the Lecture
Let's say your AI agent is already deployed in production.
Key Takeaways
  • Instead, they're logged and compared with the original versions.
  • This allows us to closely observe how the new version performs under real traffic conditions, with the same users prompts and context, without risking the actual customer experience.
  • After collecting the results from the new shadow version, we can analyze the data to understand how the changes impacted the agent's performance, including latency, accuracy, compliance with governance rules, and overall user experience.
  • Ideally, the results indicate that the new version is reliable, making it suitable for a gradual rollout to production users.

Lesson 103: Bias and Fairness Systems

  • Agents, on the other hand, are autonomous and can change the environment.
  • Their biases don't just stay confined to words on a screen.
  • An agent's capacity to take action is its greatest advantage, but it also amplifies potential risks, since even minor reasoning biases can rapidly lead to real world consequences.
  • Furthermore, once an LLM is placed within an agentic framework, the potential for errors increases as it becomes connected to external data sources.
  • tools, and possibly other agents, creating many additional points where issues can arise.
  • It's not just the LM you need to worry about, but the entire system.

Lesson 105: How to Measure Agent Performance

When evaluating agent performance, several critical dimensions come to mind accuracy, cost, latency, safety, and ultimately overall user experience. This means we can't focus on a single metric in isolation, just as we wouldn't judge a car solely by its speed, but instead consider factors like fuel efficiency, safety, reliability, and comfort.

Core Concept

When evaluating agent performance, several critical dimensions come to mind accuracy, cost, latency, safety, and ultimately overall user experience. This means we can't focus on a single metric in isolation, just as we wouldn't judge a car solely by its speed, but instead consider factors like fuel efficiency, safety, reliability, and comfort. Evaluating AI agents requires balancing multiple dimensions rather than optimizing for just one.

Key Points

  • Increasing in agent's accuracy, for instance, might come at the cost of higher latency.
  • User satisfaction is crucial, but it must be balanced against operational expenses.
  • Likewise, a perfect, reliable system is of little value if it isn't safe for end users.
  • Each of these factors is interconnected, and it's essential to understand how they influence one another within the context of the specific use case.
  • The North Star metric, or in other words, the primary KPI to track, will differ from one use case to another.
  • If you're developing a trading agent, chances are accuracy will be your top priority.
  • The team developing an agent that interacts with high value clients will likely focus intensely on customer satisfaction and user experience.
  • We must also account for how these dimensions interact.

💡 From the Lecture

Key Takeaways
  • We must also account for how these dimensions interact.
  • Recognizing that beyond a certain level of optimization, improvements in one area almost always come at the expense of another.
  • The key is to strike the right balance for the specific use case.
  • In the following two lessons, we'll outline practical steps for measuring agent performance.

Lesson 106: Offline Benchmarks

A few lessons ago, we introduced the concept of ab shadow testing, a method used when companies want to avoid risking the user experience by exposing users to the output of a new, untested agent. The concept of offline evaluation is similar.

Core Concept

A few lessons ago, we introduced the concept of ab shadow testing, a method used when companies want to avoid risking the user experience by exposing users to the output of a new, untested agent. The concept of offline evaluation is similar. It involves measuring an agent's performance under controlled test conditions using curated datasets and predefined scenarios.

Key Points

  • Imagine you've developed a customer support agent for an e-commerce company.
  • Instead of immediately allowing it to interact with real customers, you first test it on a dataset of 500 past support tickets.
  • Each ticket is already labeled with the correct response or action, allowing you to compare the agent's output against this predefined gold standard.
  • This approach allows you to estimate the agent's success rate, including accuracy and error rate, before it ever interacts with real customers.
  • Today, several tools can automate this evaluation process.
  • Among them are lang, chain, evals, and helm.
  • The clear advantage is that it eliminates any risk of negatively impacting the experience of your existing users.
  • The drawback is that the data used is historical and may not accurately represent current business conditions.
💡 From the Lecture
Imagine you've developed a customer support agent for an e-commerce company.
💡 From the Lecture
They act as a guiding framework for the team, highlighting which areas require optimization before the agent is ready for deployment in real world situations.
Key Takeaways
  • The drawback is that the data used is historical and may not accurately represent current business conditions.
  • As a result, the effectiveness of offline benchmarks depends heavily on the quality and relevance of the sample data you select.
  • Offline benchmarks are typically used towards the middle and end stages of the development phase before launching the agent.
  • They act as a guiding framework for the team, highlighting which areas require optimization before the agent is ready for deployment in real world situations.

Lesson 112: Tokens

There's no time to waste. You've likely used ChatGPT and know it works by sending a prompt to the model and expecting a text answer. The question is how does the model make sense of this text? How does it understand the meaning of the words and their mutual connection?

Core Concept

Welcome back, everyone to this section on tokens, OpenAI models and model pricing. There's no time to waste. So let's kick things off by discussing tokens.

Key Points

  • You've likely used ChatGPT and know it works by sending a prompt to the model and expecting a text answer.
  • The question is how does the model make sense of this text?
  • How does it understand the meaning of the words and their mutual connection?
  • This, of course, is a challenging question to answer, but in this lesson we'll look at one aspect that makes this possible tokenization.
  • Tokenization is a process whereby text inputs and outputs are broken down into sequences of characters called tokens.
  • The unique tokens that an LLM operates form the vocabulary of this LM, a token amounts to roughly three quarters of a word.
  • An easier way of remembering this is to consider that 100 tokens corresponds to approximately 75 words.
  • So when talking about OpenAI's tokenizing mechanism, a token isn't necessarily a single character or a word, but rather a sequence of characters frequently seen together.

  • What token differs from the IDs of the first and second one?
  • Okay, I hope you now have a good understanding of what tokens are.

Lesson 116: Setting the API Key as an Environment Variable

Hey, in the previous lesson, we logged into OpenAI's website, generated a personal API key, and saved it locally in a text file. We'll learn how to set this API key as an environment variable, which will soon be used to communicate with the OpenAI library.

Core Concept

Hey, in the previous lesson, we logged into OpenAI's website, generated a personal API key, and saved it locally in a text file. We'll learn how to set this API key as an environment variable, which will soon be used to communicate with the OpenAI library. First, let's delve into the concept of environment variables.

Key Points

  • An environment variable is a key value pair used by the operating system, with the key corresponding to the name of the variable, while the value representing, in our case the OpenAI API key.
  • The key and the value are typically stored as strings.
  • A classic example is the path environment variable, which stores a list of directories where executable programs are located, enabling the operating system to find these programs when needed.
  • Another typical example is the home or home path environment variable, storing the path to the user's home directory.
  • Environment variables are essential for protecting such sensitive data as API keys.
  • For example, the OpenAI API key, a required credential for accessing the OpenAI services, should not be exposed within the code.
  • Hard coding its value risks unintended exposure, such as when you share your code with friends or colleagues.
  • This is a critical security issue because invoking OpenAI's models through the API corresponds to using tokens, a paid service.

Lesson 118: System, User, and Assistant Roles

Last time we started creating our chat completion object, we left it off at the messages parameter, a list of dictionaries where we can specify prompts as a system, a user or an assistant. The system role is typically used for directing the model.

Core Concept

Last time we started creating our chat completion object, we left it off at the messages parameter, a list of dictionaries where we can specify prompts as a system, a user or an assistant. Let's now discuss each of these roles individually. The system role is typically used for directing the model.

Key Points

  • It defines the model's purpose, persona, output, format, and any other necessary instructions.
  • Providing the bot with a system message guarantees a better response for your specific use case.
  • For instance, if you were to create a grammar corrector, an appropriate system message would be you will be provided with statements and your task is to convert them to standard English.
  • If you were to create a chatbot with a sarcastic twist instead, you could give it the following instructions.
  • You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly answers questions with sarcastic responses.
  • For more ideas on possible system prompts, refer to OpenAI's web page.
  • The second role on our list is the user role.
  • The content you pass as a user can range from a question you need answered to a sentence you want extended to a paragraph requiring grammar corrections, and much more.

Creating a Sarcastic Chatbot

Welcome back, everyone! In this lesson, we’ll resume the implementation of our chat completion in Jupyter Notebook. We’ll start by instructing the chatbot to answer questions sarcastically through a system message and then pass our question as a user-role message. Let’s get into it! For starters, run the first four code cells below.

Step 1 
import os
import openai
Step 2 
openai.api_key = os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')
Step 3 
client = openai.OpenAI()

Now, the first dictionary in our messages list should map the ‘role’ keyword to ‘system’, implying a system message. In addition, set the content to the one already familiar to you: *You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly answers questions with sarcastic responses.* In the second dictionary in the list, we’ll create a user message. I’ll go with the following request: *I’ve recently adopted a dog. Could you suggest some dog names?*

Step 4 
completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'system', 
                                                         'content':''' You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly 
                                                         answers questions with sarcastic responses. '''}, 
                                                        {'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' I've recently adopted a dog. 
                                                         Could you suggest some dog names? '''}])

Run the cell above and inspect the completion variable.

Step 5 
completion

We find that completion is an instance of the ChatCompletion class, with the parameter choices storing a list of Choice objects that, in turn, keep the responses from the chatbot. By default, the model returns only one response, which is typically the desired setting. This number can be controlled through a parameter called n. Of course, more responses result in higher token consumption and, therefore, higher cost. The role assigned to this message is ‘assistant.’ Additionally, information is available on the number of completion, prompt, and total tokens.

Finally, for this lesson, let’s check how the chatbot responded by displaying the output in a more readable form. To do that:

  • first, retrieve the choices list from the ChatCompletion object,
  • then select the first and only item in this list,
  • fetch the messages parameter from the Choice object,
  • and lastly, extract the content from the ChatCompletionMessage object.
Make sure you apply the print-function to the string to ensure the message is nicely formatted.

Step 6 
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)

Excellent job, everyone. In the upcoming lesson, we’ll discuss additional parameters that can help further control the model’s response. See you in a bit!

Lesson 120: Temperature, Max Tokens, and Streaming

We then used a system message to create a chatbot that adopts a sarcastic persona. As discussed earlier, OpenAI sets its model prices based on the number of input tokens. The ones we feed to the model and the number of completion tokens those the model generates.

Core Concept

In this section, we've discussed the roles we can employ when passing a message to a model, a system user or assistant role. We then used a system message to create a chatbot that adopts a sarcastic persona. Let's begin with the tokens.

Key Points

  • As discussed earlier, OpenAI sets its model prices based on the number of input tokens.
  • The ones we feed to the model and the number of completion tokens those the model generates.
  • Both are capped to prevent users from inputting an excessive number of tokens, and to stop the models from generating endless text.
  • Still, it's essential to have additional control over the amount of text generated.
  • Models often tend to be wordy and provide more information than needed.
  • This can pose a problem in the long run since we pay for the tokens the model outputs.
  • As a side note, this pricing only applies when using OpenAI's models through the API.
  • In contrast, the ChatGPT platform is subscription based rather than token based, and you don't need to worry about the model generating long texts.

💻 Code Walkthrough: 04-The-OpenAI-API-04.ipynb

▶ Show Code Walkthrough (52 lines)

Temperature, Max Tokens, and Streaming

Welcome back! In this section, we’ve discussed the roles we can employ when passing a message to a model: a system, user, or assistant role. We then used a system message to create a chatbot that adopts a sarcastic persona. In this lesson, we’ll discuss a few more parameters that can affect the model’s response:

  • Its maximum number of completion tokens,
  • Level of randomness, and
  • The option to stream it.
Let’s begin with the tokens. As discussed earlier, OpenAI sets its model prices based on the number of input tokens (the ones we feed to the model) and the number of completion tokens (those the model generates). Both are capped to prevent users from inputting an excessive number of tokens and to stop the models from generating endless text. Still, it’s essential to have additional control over the amount of text generated. Models often tend to be wordy and provide more information than needed. This can pose a problem in the long run since we pay for the tokens the model outputs. As a side note, this pricing only applies when using OpenAI’s models through the API. In contrast, the ChatGPT platform is subscription-based rather than token-based, and you don’t need to worry about the model generating long texts. All right. It’s time we see the token parameter in action!

Step 1 
import os
import openai
Step 2 
openai.api_key = os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')
Step 3 
client = openai.OpenAI()

When defining the completion variable, keep the system message the same. However, let’s test the model with a different user message. For example: *Could you explain briefly what a black hole is?* Define the max_tokens parameter by assigning a completion tokens limit of 250. Run the cell and print out the content.

Step 4 
completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'system', 
                                                         'content':''' You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly 
                                                         answers questions with sarcastic responses. '''}, 
                                                        {'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250)
Step 5 
completion

As always, our sarcastic chatbot gives an excellent response. 😊

Let’s now see how it performs when we narrow the cap down to 50 tokens.

Step 6 
completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'system', 
                                                         'content':''' You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly 
                                                         answers questions with sarcastic responses. '''}, 
                                                        {'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 50)
Step 7 
completion

This time, we get a much shorter (maybe even incomplete) response. So, we need to be careful not to limit the model too much.

I’ll now revert to 250 completion tokens. Another parameter we’ll use throughout the course is temperature. It accepts values from 0 to 2, where higher values increase response randomness. Although it defaults to 1, let's explore its behavior at the extremes. Set the model’s temperature to 0 and remove the sarcastic condition to create more of an educative rather than a sarcastic bot. Let’s again ask it to explain what black holes are.

Step 8 
completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250, 
                                            temperature = 0)
Step 9 
completion

We obtain an informative response. Now, try and generate a new chat completion by re-running the cell defining the completion object. Display the variable. We find the new response is similar to the previous one. Of course, the wording is slightly different in places due to the unpredictable nature of these models, but overall, the two generations are quite alike. Models with lower temperatures can be used when creating a chatbot for educational purposes because the answers must be more academic and informative rather than creative.

Okay, let’s now increase the temperature to maximum and study these results.

Step 10 
completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250, 
                                            temperature = 2)
Step 11 
completion

Well, we can all agree that this is far from helpful. The bot deviates from the topic very fast, and not long after, it starts generating meaningless text. So, such large temperature values are rarely helpful.

I’ll switch back to a temperature value of zero.

Another parameter that controls determinism is seed—like the seeds we’ve fed to machine learning algorithms for reproducibility. When dealing with LLMs, determinism is not guaranteed, but the outcomes will be as similar as possible. (You can experiment with this parameter at home.) From now on, I’ll set the temperature parameter to 0 and seed to 365 . I suggest you do the same to obtain results like mine.

Step 12 
completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250, 
                                            temperature = 0, 
                                            seed = 365)

Okay, moving on! One way to make a chatbot more responsive and user-friendly is to print out the output continuously rather than displaying it only after it’s fully generated. The stream parameter allows us to achieve precisely that. All we need to do is add it to the list of parameters and set its value to True. Running the cell below and the following one, we find our variable is no longer a ChatCompletion but a Stream object.

Step 13 
completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250, 
                                            temperature = 0, 
                                            seed = 365, 
                                            stream = True)
Step 14 
completion

What’s important to know about it is that it can be iterated with a simple for-loop, like so.

Step 15 
for i in completion:
    print(i)

Executing the cell, we find a long list of ChatCompletionChunk objects. As their name suggests, they contain only a small chunk of the message. Now, within the for-loop, let’s print the content of each chunk. Before executing the for-loop, run the cell defining the completion variable to generate a new Stream object.

Step 16 
for i in completion:
    print(i.choices[0].delta.content, end = "")

Look at that! We’ve managed to stream our text on the screen. How cool is that? 😊

This marks the end of our short introduction to the OpenAI API. I’m convinced you now find creating a chatbot with APIs much more fun and rewarding than merely chatting with ChatGPT. It gives you much more control over the responses and allows you to create some exciting chatbots. But wait until you see what LangChain has to offer. 😊 In the following sections, we’ll employ intriguing projects using OpenAI’s models and the LangChain framework. Until then! 😊

Lesson 123: System and Human Messages

In the previous lesson, we constructed a simple chatbot using the chat OpenAI class in Lang chain to invoke the model. We passed a single string containing our request and got an AI message object in return.

Core Concept

Welcome back everyone. In the previous lesson, we constructed a simple chatbot using the chat OpenAI class in Lang chain to invoke the model. We passed a single string containing our request and got an AI message object in return.

Key Points

  • But Lang Chain enables us to invoke chat models in several other ways.
  • In this lesson, we'll dig a bit deeper into the system and human roles, which act like the system and user roles we encountered in the OpenAI API.
  • To refresh your memory, these message roles specify the messages sender.
  • A system message directs the model's behavior, such as emulating a teenager, an academic, or a philosopher.
  • For instance, you can find an example on OpenAI's web page like this.
  • You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly answers questions with sarcastic responses.
  • On the other hand, human messages are messages sent by the user questions or requests that require a response from the model.
  • Having revised the concepts, let's outline the strategy for this lesson.
💡 From the Lecture
For instance, you can find an example on OpenAI's web page like this.

System and Human Messages

Step 1

Step 3

from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage
Step 4

                  model_kwargs = {'seed':365},

Lesson 125: Prompt Templates and Prompt Values

We've explored and tested Lang chains chat open AI class. We meticulously examined the invoke method, noting that it accepts a string or a list of chat messages when used on chat. The chat messages we analyzed included a system message storing instructions for the model, a human message storing the user's questions or request, and an AI message storing the models or example responses.

Core Concept

We've explored and tested Lang chains chat open AI class. We meticulously examined the invoke method, noting that it accepts a string or a list of chat messages when used on chat. Open AI object.

Key Points

  • The chat messages we analyzed included a system message storing instructions for the model, a human message storing the user's questions or request, and an AI message storing the models or example responses.
  • These message objects proved very useful but have a significant drawback they are not reusable.
  • The developers at Lang Chain have therefore implemented prompt abstractions called chat prompt templates, allowing for the reuse of system, human and AI messages.
  • Before jumping into chat prompt templates, however, discussing prompt templates constructed from simple strings rather than chat messages will be helpful.
  • Open a clean notebook in the Lang chain environment.
  • Begin by defining a variable called template.
  • You'll notice some developers adhere to the convention of using all caps for string templates.
  • Let's apply this convention to our code as well.

Lesson 127: Few-Shot Chat Message Prompt Templates

OpenAI objects how to employ system human and AI messages, how prompt templates work, and how they differ from chat prompt templates. Additionally, we observed that the output of one invoke method could serve as the argument to another.

Core Concept

So far in this section we've learned how to create and use chat. OpenAI objects how to employ system human and AI messages, how prompt templates work, and how they differ from chat prompt templates. Additionally, we observed that the output of one invoke method could serve as the argument to another.

Key Points

  • More specifically, the chat value object resulting from the invocation of a chat prompt template instance could serve as an argument to the invoke method of a chat.
  • Let's now revisit the lesson where we created two human AI message pairs, which taught the model to answer questions sarcastically.
  • We refer to this as few shot prompting, giving the model a couple of examples to learn from.
  • This would be a zero shot prompting if we provided no examples to the model.
  • I think we can all agree that this previous implementation of few shot prompting was somewhat clumsy.
  • Our approach was to define a separate human AI messages pair for each example.
  • This needlessly cluttered the code and is evidently hardly scalable.
  • In this lesson, we'll utilize a class called few Shot Chatmessage prompt template and recreate the same example, but implemented much cleaner and more compactly.

Few-Shot Chat Message Prompt Templates

Step 1 
# Run the line of code below to check the version of langchain in the current environment.

Step 2 
pip show langchain
Step 3 
from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI

from langchain_core.prompts import (ChatPromptTemplate,
                                    HumanMessagePromptTemplate, 
                                    AIMessagePromptTemplate, 
                                    FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate)
Step 4 
chat = ChatOpenAI(model_name = 'gpt-4', 
                  model_kwargs = {'seed':365},
                  temperature = 0,
                  max_tokens = 100)
Step 5

Could you suggest some {pet} names?'''
TEMPLATE_AI = '''{response}'''

message_template_h = HumanMessagePromptTemplate.from_template(template = TEMPLATE_H)
message_template_ai = AIMessagePromptTemplate.from_template(template = TEMPLATE_AI)
Step 6 
example_template = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([message_template_h, 
                                                     message_template_ai])
Step 7 
examples = [{'pet':'dog', 
             'response':'''Oh, absolutely. Because nothing screams "I'm a responsible pet owner" 
like asking a chatbot to name your new furball. How about "Bark Twain" (if it's a literary hound)? '''}, 
            
            {'pet':'cat', 
             'response':'''Oh, absolutely. Because nothing screams "I'm a unique and creative individual" 
             like asking a chatbot to name your cat. How about "Furry McFurFace", "Sir Meowsalot", or "Catastrophe"? '''}, 
            
            {'pet':'fish', 
             'response':
             '''Oh, absolutely. Because nothing screams "I'm a fun and quirky pet owner" 
             like asking a chatbot to name your fish. How about "Fin Diesel", "Gill Gates", or "Bubbles"?'''}]
Step 8 
few_shot_prompt = FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate(examples = examples, 
                                                   example_prompt = example_template, 
                                                   input_variables = ['pet'])
Step 9 
chat_template = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([few_shot_prompt, 
                                                  message_template_h])
Step 10 
chat_value = chat_template.invoke({'pet':'rabbit'})
Step 11 
chat_value
Step 12 
for i in chat_value.messages:
    print(f'{i.type}: {i.content}\n')
Step 13 
response = chat.invoke(chat_value)
Step 14 
response
Step 15 
print(response.content)
Key Takeaways
  • Invoke chat template to redefine the chat value object and invoke the chat model to generate an even better response because of the increased number of examples.
  • This approach avoids defining a series of message objects and instead uses only a handful of prompt templates.
  • This concludes our lesson on prompting.
  • Looking forward to meeting you in the next section.

Lesson 131: Piping a Prompt, Model, and an Output Parser

Lang chain expression language is a way of grouping chains out of individual components known as runnable. These components and the resulting chain support a standard set of invocation methods invoke stream, batch and their asynchronous analogues.

Core Concept

Welcome back everyone. Lang chain expression language is a way of grouping chains out of individual components known as runnable. These components and the resulting chain support a standard set of invocation methods invoke stream, batch and their asynchronous analogues.

Key Points

  • You're already familiar with the invoke method that connects one component's output with another's input.
  • The stream method ensures that a completion token is printed out as soon as it's generated, making the application you're building more user friendly and responsive.
  • The batch method, intuitively, is in control of handling more than one input.
  • Finally, the topic of asynchronous methods, while not covered in this course, is notably accessible at no extra cost through Lang Chain Expression Language implementation.
  • In this lesson, we'll create and invoke a chain with the familiar but slightly modified question.
  • The desired output would be to have the names as the elements of a list object.
  • As usual, I've prepared a notebook with much of the code pre implemented.
  • Let me walk you through the implementation.

Welcome back everyone. Last lesson we saw how easily chains were created in the Lang chain expression language. Recall that it uses a pipe symbol to connect components.

Key Points

Batching

Step 1 
# Run the line of code below to check the version of langchain in the current environment.
# Substitute "langchain" with any other package name to check their version.
Step 2 
pip show langchain
Step 3 
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
Step 4 
chat_template = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ('human', 
     "I've recently adopted a {pet} which is a {breed}. Could you suggest several training tips?")])
Step 5 
chat = ChatOpenAI(model_name = 'gpt-4', 
                  model_kwargs = {'seed':365},
                  temperature = 0,
                  max_tokens = 100)
Step 6 
chain = chat_template | chat
Step 7 
chain.invoke({'pet':'dog', 'breed':'shepherd'})
Step 8 
%%time
chain.batch([{'pet':'dog', 'breed':'shepherd'}, 
             {'pet':'dragon', 'breed':'night fury'}])
Step 9 
%%time
chain.invoke({'pet':'dog', 'breed':'shepherd'})
Step 10 
%%time
chain.invoke({'pet':'dragon', 'breed':'night fury'})
Key Takeaways
  • Therefore, we can confidently conclude that passing several inputs at once to a batch method is much more time efficient than invoking the chain that many times in sequence.
  • You can imagine how this can scale up significantly with more dictionaries and lengthier responses.
  • All right, I'll end our discussion on the batch method here.
  • In the following lessons, we'll continue with the streaming process.

Lesson 133: Streaming

Last lesson we revised the invoke method and learned about its close cousin, the batch method, which allows for invoking a chain with more than a single response quickly and efficiently. We'll dedicate this lesson to the third and final method included in the expression language's standard interface stream.

Core Concept

Welcome back everyone. Last lesson we revised the invoke method and learned about its close cousin, the batch method, which allows for invoking a chain with more than a single response quickly and efficiently. We'll dedicate this lesson to the third and final method included in the expression language's standard interface stream.

Key Points

  • Open the last session's notebook or a duplicate.
  • Paste either code for invoking a chain and substitute the invoke method with stream instead.
  • Running the cell, we get an output that should look familiar.
  • Recall that we encountered generators back when we covered OpenAI's API.
  • Let's expand our knowledge and share additional insight into these fascinating objects.
  • Generator functions in Python allow for defining functions that behave like iterators, allowing us to loop over their output.
  • Unlike standard functions, generators preserve their local state and each subsequent invocation picks up where the last one left off.
  • This is achieved through a yield statement that produces a sequence of values instead of a return statement, which exits a function altogether.

💻 Code Walkthrough: 08-LCEL-03.ipynb

Streaming

Step 1 
# Run the line of code below to check the version of langchain in the current environment.
# Substitute "langchain" with any other package name to check their version.
Step 2 
pip show langchain
Step 3 
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
Step 4 
chat_template = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ('human', 
     "I've recently adopted a {pet} which is a {breed}. Could you suggest several training tips?")])
Step 5 
chat = ChatOpenAI(model_name = 'gpt-4', 
                  model_kwargs = {'seed':365},
                  temperature = 0,
                  max_tokens = 100)
Step 6 
chain = chat_template | chat
Step 7 
chain.invoke({'pet':'dog', 'breed':'shepherd'})
Step 8 
%%time
chain.batch([{'pet':'dog', 'breed':'shepherd'}, 
             {'pet':'dragon', 'breed':'night fury'}])
Step 9 
%%time
chain.invoke({'pet':'dog', 'breed':'shepherd'})
Step 10 
%%time
chain.invoke({'pet':'dragon', 'breed':'night fury'})
Step 11 
response = chain.stream({'pet':'dragon', 'breed':'night fury'})
Step 12 
next(response)
Step 13 
for i in response:
    print(i.content, end = '')

  • We've laid the foundation of the Lang chain expression language.

Lesson 139: RunnableLambda

So far you've acquired much knowledge about the Lang Chain expression language and its underlying mechanism. We talked about the runnable class implementing the invoke batch and stream methods. Instances of this class can be composed to create runnable sequences, also known as chains.

Core Concept

Lesson 140: The @chain Decorator

The @chain Decorator

Step 1 
# Run the line of code below to check the version of langchain in the current environment.

Step 2 
pip show langchain
Step 3 
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda
from langchain_core.runnables import chain
Step 4 
def find_sum(x):
    return sum(x)

def find_square(x):
    return x**2
Step 5 
chain1 = RunnableLambda(find_sum) | RunnableLambda(find_square)
Step 6

Step 7 
@chain
def runnable_sum(x):
    return sum(x)

@chain
def runnable_square(x):
    return x**2
Step 8 
type(runnable_sum), type(runnable_square)
Step 9 
chain2 = runnable_sum | runnable_square
Step 10 
chain2.invoke([1, 2, 5])

Lesson 141: How to Integrate Custom Data into an LLM

Now that you've acquired solid experience with LMS, I hope you can see that these are powerful, state of the art models trained on vast amounts of data and answering questions on various topics. The models are rapidly becoming better and more knowledgeable, but training them takes a lot of time, so the data available to LMS inevitably has a cut off date.   • The most straightforward way to provide a model with personal data is to feed the information directly through prompting.
  • This means inserting the data as a system message, a set of few shot examples, a chat history, or however appropriate.
  • You then pass these prompts to a model, as we've done many times.
  • This approach is quick and easy to implement.

Lesson 143: Introduction to Document Loading and Splitting

In the last lesson, we provided an overview of the retrieval augmented generation technique and learned that it consists of three main parts indexing, retrieval, and generation. The first part in turn comprises the following steps document loading, splitting, embedding and storing.

Core Concept

Welcome back everyone. In the last lesson, we provided an overview of the retrieval augmented generation technique and learned that it consists of three main parts indexing, retrieval, and generation. The first part in turn comprises the following steps document loading, splitting, embedding and storing.

Key Points

  • We'll dedicate this lesson to the first two steps document loading and splitting.
  • Document loaders in long chain are classes responsible for taking a data source, a PDF, HTML, JSON, or virtually any other standard format, scraping its content and saving it as a list of document objects.
  • Document is a class in Lang chain used to store a piece of text and its associated metadata, such as page number, document title and document subtitle, among others.
  • Converting data from any format to a uniform structure might sound straightforward, but document loaders are an essential and involved component of a Rag application.
  • This standardization means that all files are handled identically in later stages, despite the diversity of their original formats.
  • Lang chain supports integration with many file formats and can load data directly from various file storage platforms such as Google Drive and Dropbox.
  • The practical part of this section demonstrates how to load content from PDF and doc files.
  • You're then encouraged to experiment by applying the same process to other file extensions, and noting the different metadata extracted from these files.
💡 From the Lecture
This means we need to find a mechanism that not only splits the data into chunks to decrease the document's length, but also ensures that each chunk is centered around one topic, as we'll discover in the upcoming lessons.
Key Takeaways
  • So far, we've covered the process of loading a text file and splitting it into meaningful chunks that fit the context window limit of a model.
  • We now want to create a chatbot that answers user questions based on the information stored in these chunks.
  • To answer the question most efficiently, without needing to go through each split individually, we seek a mechanism that locates the one semantically closest to the user question.
  • The technique for that is called embedding and will be the next lesson's topic.

Lesson 144: Introduction to Document Embedding

In the last lesson, we started our discussion by focusing on the first two components of the indexing part. Document loading and splitting. We realized the need for a mechanism that swiftly identifies the most relevant chunks for a given question.

Core Concept

In the last lesson, we started our discussion by focusing on the first two components of the indexing part. Document loading and splitting. We realized the need for a mechanism that swiftly identifies the most relevant chunks for a given question.

Key Points

  • Embedding a text is a process whereby a language model converts it to a vector, effectively capturing its semantic meaning in a numerical format.
  • With the help of these vectors, we can perform similarity searches efficiently.
  • This likely sounds unintuitive, but it's an approach that works impressively well for llms.
  • Let's study a simple example and conceptually discuss the meaning behind vector representations.
  • Imagine we have two vectors, each representing a chunk of text, one containing the keyword star and another son.
  • When positioned on a coordinate system, these vectors would sit closely together because they have close semantic meaning and are often used in the same context.
  • Conversely, segments with spaghetti and Bolognese are distant from the earlier pairs, yet closely related, as these terms frequently co-occur but seldom align with star and sun.
  • Let's now position a third pair of text chunks on the coordinate system.

  • But considering we're expressing something as complicated as human language, this number is insignificant.
  • In the practical part of this section, we'll embed text chunks and compare different dot products.

Lesson 148: Indexing: Document Splitting with Character Text Splitter (Theory)

As we've discussed, splitting a document into semantically meaningful chunks is essential in the Rag process. It helps reduce the text size, ensuring it will fit a model's context window limit and segments the text into chunks of specific topics, which improves the quality of the chatbot's responses.

Core Concept

Hey everyone, welcome to this series of lessons on document splitting. As we've discussed, splitting a document into semantically meaningful chunks is essential in the Rag process. It helps reduce the text size, ensuring it will fit a model's context window limit and segments the text into chunks of specific topics, which improves the quality of the chatbot's responses.

Key Points

  • Lang chain offers various algorithms for splitting a document.
  • Let's begin with splitting governed by a predefined number of characters, which means we obtain chunks of roughly equal sizes before jumping to coding.
  • However, I think we should discuss this idea conceptually through a simple example.
  • Imagine we're given a text containing 1500 characters.
  • Please pay attention to the fact that we're referring to characters, not tokens or words.
  • In that way, we've reduced the size of the documents from 1500 to 500 characters, at the cost of increasing their number.
  • Another parameter we can specify is the chunk overlap.
  • Chunk overlap corresponds to the number of characters overlapping between subsequent chunks.
💡 From the Lecture
Imagine we're given a text containing 1500 characters.
💡 From the Lecture
We can now design a splitter separating the text into chunks with a maximum of, for example, 500 characters each, resulting in three chunks of equal sizes.
Key Takeaways
  • Since we still have some text left over, the fourth and final chunk begins with the last 50 characters from the third split, and then takes the remaining 100 from the text.
  • Therefore, introducing a chunk overlap increases the number of splits, but it has the benefit of including context from the previous split to the next, thereby introducing a smoother flow between the chunks.
  • Okay, we've covered the conceptual part of the character splitting technique.
  • It's time we realized it in code in the next lesson.

Step 2

Step 3 
from langchain_community.document_loaders import Docx2txtLoader
from langchain_text_splitters.markdown import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter
from langchain_text_splitters.character import CharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_openai.embeddings import OpenAIEmbeddings
import numpy as np
Step 4 
loader_docx = Docx2txtLoader("Introduction_to_Data_and_Data_Science_2.docx")
pages = loader_docx.load()

md_splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(
    headers_to_split_on = [("#", "Course Title"), 
                           ("##", "Lecture Title")]
)

pages_md_split = md_splitter.split_text(pages[0].page_content)

for i in range(len(pages_md_split)):
    pages_md_split[i].page_content = ' '.join(pages_md_split[i].page_content.split())
    
char_splitter = CharacterTextSplitter(
    separator = ".",
    chunk_size = 500,
    chunk_overlap  = 50
)

pages_char_split = char_splitter.split_documents(pages_md_split)
Step 5 
pages_char_split
Step 6 
embedding = OpenAIEmbeddings(model = "text-embedding-ada-002")
Step 7 
pages_char_split[18]

vector2 = embedding.embed_query(pages_char_split[5].page_content)
vector3 = embedding.embed_query(pages_char_split[18].page_content)
Step 9 
len(vector1), len(vector2), len(vector3)
Step 10 
np.dot(vector1, vector2), np.dot(vector1, vector3), np.dot(vector2, vector3)
Step 11 
np.linalg.norm(vector1), np.linalg.norm(vector2), np.linalg.norm(vector3)
Key Takeaways
  • Rerun the cell, this time with vectors two and three.
  • Keep in mind that in this lesson we embedded only three of a total of 20 chunks.
  • Therefore, we're starting to feel the need for a vector database to store these embeddings.
  • That will be precisely the topic of our next lesson.
